In one sentence: blockchain engineers are not about buying coins or issuing a token; they maintain and support distributed, decentralized blockchain networks or blockchain applications, design and deploy secure blockchain design patterns and cryptographic protocols, and test their security, performance, and failure boundaries before and after deployment. The U.S. counterpart is O*NET-SOC 15-1299.07, marked Bright Outlook and listed as Job Zone Four (considerable preparation needed, SVP 7.0 to less than 8.0). The core boundary is that you can decide technical approaches at the protocol and implementation level, but you cannot make compliance, funding, or external disclosure decisions for the institution, and you cannot treat the chain running normally as meaning that business and compliance risks are already resolved.

Signals to keep exploring: you are willing to first write what needs to be solved as verifiable requirements and a threat list and only then write code; you can accept having your contracts, node configurations, and deployment scripts reviewed line by line by others; when key management, access control, exception handling, or performance bottlenecks arise, you are willing to stop and do small-scale testing and recording rather than getting the feature running and shipping it; and your interest in under what conditions the system fails and how large the consequences are exceeds your interest in whether the feature was built.

Conditions for pausing major investment: you have not yet completed, in a controlled environment (a testnet or a self-built environment), one full closed loop of requirements, design, implementation, testing, deployment, monitoring, and emergency response; or you only want to copy an existing template into a system that can be demonstrated and are unwilling to bear responsibility for keys, permissions, and change records; also, do not treat knowing one smart contract language or having taken a few online courses as proof that you can independently take responsibility for production environment funds and data security.

Education, qualifications, and job authorization must be verified separately: O*NET lists this occupation as Job Zone Four (SVP 7.0 to less than 8.0), and among respondents 38% consider a bachelor's degree necessary, 19% consider some college education without a degree necessary, and 13% consider a master's degree necessary; the O*NET education and training information is not a list of occupational licenses, and entry conditions must be verified separately by the target jurisdiction, service content, and employer requirements. These are survey and public material definitions, not statutory thresholds; real requirements follow the employer, the project client, and local regulations, and production release authority and key custody authority additionally require institutional authorization.

In one sentence: this is a technical role centered on distributed ledgers, cryptographic protocols, node and deployment security, and testing and monitoring, and its output is reviewable, reproducible, and rollback-capable systems and evidence, not investment advice or compliance judgments made on behalf of the institution. The work of blockchain engineers falls into three categories: first, design and protocol tasks (discussing and planning systems with solution architects, systems engineers, or cybersecurity experts, designing and validating cryptographic protocols, and designing blockchain design patterns that make transactions secure, transparent, and tamper-resistant); second, implementation and deployment tasks (writing maintainable code using object-oriented design principles, updating client and server applications, designing data repositories, and automating deployment of updates across geographically distributed nodes); third, testing and risk tasks (testing the security and performance of blockchain infrastructure, assessing threats such as untested code and unprotected keys, running infrastructure tests to examine the behavior of large peer-to-peer networks, and implementing failure handling and logging). All three share the same reviewable chain of evidence.
Design and protocol tasks

Clarify client or business requirements → determine system boundaries and the threat model with architects and systems and security personnel → design blockchain design patterns and cryptographic protocols → define the data and permission model → review the control matrix and risk assessment results → produce implementable specifications and a deployment plan.
Implementation and deployment tasks

Write maintainable code according to object-oriented design principles → update integration and business logic in client and server applications → design and implement data repositories → implement logging and monitoring → automate deployment of updates across geographically distributed nodes through CI and configuration management → retain version, configuration, and rollback records.

Test the security and performance of blockchain infrastructure in a controlled environment, run infrastructure tests to examine peer-to-peer network behavior at scale, assess threats such as untested code and unprotected keys, implement catastrophic failure handlers to identify security intrusions promptly, review assessment processes and risks based on security assessments or the control matrix, and finally write the conclusions and limitations clearly.

Blockchain engineers center on the technical implementation of distributed ledgers and cryptographic protocols: information security analysts (15-1212.00) face broader information system security protection and compliance and do not take ledger protocols as their default subject; computer systems analysts (15-1211.00) focus on analyzing and improving business systems and do not necessarily handle cryptography and consensus; database administrators (15-1242.00) work around data storage and queries; computer programmers (15-1251.00) mainly write and test code, and their official definition does not include blockchain protocol and consensus design by default; penetration testers (15-1299.04) center on authorized attack simulation. Similar job titles do not mean responsibilities are interchangeable. Database administrators 15-1242.00 and the architect classification are different, and the two are not combined into one precise occupation for wages or duties.
Core purpose
Keep distributed networks and blockchain applications running stably on a secure, transparent, and verifiable basis, and make every transaction and change traceable.
Main subjects and basis

The subjects are distributed ledger networks, nodes, smart contracts and client and server applications, and key and permission configurations; the basis is system requirements and the threat model, protocol and design pattern specifications, security assessments and the control matrix, and applicable regulations and platform rules.
Core process

Clarifying requirements and threats, designing protocols and design patterns, implementing coding and data models, distributed deployment and automation, security and performance testing, monitoring and failure handling, and change and rollback records.
Main outputs

Maintainable code and contracts, protocol and design pattern descriptions, deployment and configuration scripts, testing and security assessment records, monitoring and logging plans, and technical documentation including limitations and rollback notes.
Responsible party

The protocol and implementation level is the responsibility of trained and authorized engineering personnel; funding, compliance, and external disclosure decisions are the responsibility of the institution and its compliance, risk control, and legal roles; when work exceeds your authorization (for example production release, key custody, or external statements) you should escalate rather than decide on your own.
Permissions and approval

Whether you may access the production environment and mainnet, whether you may hold or custody keys, and whether you may release and upgrade contracts are determined jointly by the institutional authorization chain, change approval, and applicable regulations, and do not arise automatically from technical ability or job grade.
Conclusion boundaries

Testing and assessment conclusions describe the properties the system exhibits and the known limitations under a given configuration and test conditions; they are not the same as absolute security and do not replace compliance, funding, or legal judgment, and are affected by test coverage, environment differences, and version changes.

Before starting, verify at least six items: the occupation definition and the job entity, the education and training pathway, the actual languages and toolchains used, access authorization for the production environment and keys, the review mechanism for code and changes, and the real pay structure and on-call arrangements.
Occupation definition

Item 86 of the 2026 public notice by the Fuzhou Human Resources and Social Security Bureau actually lists blockchain engineering technicians (2-02-38-08); when the Cyberspace Administration of China republished it in 2020 the code was 2-02-10-15, describing architecture, underlying technology, applications, testing, deployment, and operations. The original 2022 code entry returned no body text this round, and no claim is made that the full text was read. Classification is not the same as an individual license, and a same-named Chinese position does not prove one-to-one correspondence with U.S. 15-1299.07.
Education and training pathway

O*NET lists it as Job Zone Four (SVP 7.0 to less than 8.0), and respondents consider a bachelor's degree necessary at 38%, some college education without a degree at 19%, and a master's degree at 13%; coursework and training in computer science, software engineering, cryptography, and information security are common foundations, and the O*NET education and training information is not a list of occupational licenses; entry conditions must be verified separately by the target jurisdiction, service content, and employer requirements.
Methods and tools

The O*NET technology list groups software and tools into 21 categories and marks 34 Hot Technologies and 20 In-Demand skills; common areas include containers and orchestration (Docker, Kubernetes), development languages and runtimes (Go, C and C++, Java, C#, TypeScript, Node.js), cloud and configuration management (AWS, Azure, Terraform, Ansible), databases and messaging (MySQL, PostgreSQL, MongoDB, Kafka), and version control and collaboration (Git, JIRA, Confluence); the labels indicate frequency of appearance in job postings, tools are only means of implementation, and protocol choices and security conclusions still rest with people.
Key and data authorization

On-chain data is hard to delete once written, and keys and credentials are hard to revoke once leaked; verify key custody and rotation rules, environment isolation, access control, and audit logs, and confirm whether the cloud services or third-party tools used are permitted to process the relevant data.
Records and review

Editorial suggestion: bring code, contracts, configurations, and deployment scripts under version control, and arrange review, staged release, and failure handling suited to the actual system. It was not verified that all employers have a two-person review system; distinguish reversible code and configuration changes from transactions already written to the ledger, and do not use release records to promise reversal of on-chain results.
Pay and working hours

The same job title may be paid by annual salary, by project, or under a service contract; when comparing, include production permissions and key responsibilities, on-call and emergency response arrangements, the change approval burden, continuing learning costs, and whether there is mentoring by senior personnel in the written agreement.

Blockchain engineers (U.S. counterpart O*NET-SOC 15-1299.07, Blockchain Engineers) maintain and support distributed, decentralized blockchain networks or blockchain applications (such as cryptocurrency transactions, payment processing, document sharing, and digital voting); they use advanced technology to design and deploy secure blockchain design patterns and solutions across geographically distributed networks; and they may assist with infrastructure setup and testing to keep applications transparent and secure. It is neither a trading or investment position nor one that bears compliance approval responsibility.

O*NET occupational identity and tasks: O*NET-SOC 15-1299.07 Blockchain Engineers, Bright Outlook, updated 2026, Job Zone Four (SVP 7.0 to less than 8.0). The official duty is to maintain and support distributed and decentralized blockchain networks or blockchain applications and to design and deploy secure blockchain design patterns and solutions across geographically distributed networks; there are 18 tasks in total, of which 17 are Core with importance ratings, and the new API task has an unpublished importance rating rather than 0; the high-importance tasks include discussing and planning systems with architects, systems engineers, or cybersecurity experts (92), implementing catastrophic failure handlers to identify security intrusions (91), testing the security and performance of blockchain infrastructure (91), assessing threats such as untested code and unprotected keys (88), and designing and deploying design patterns that make transactions secure, transparent, and tamper-resistant (85).

This definition is not a separate 15-1299.07 statistic.

paragraphs: This page compares blockchain engineers with five adjacent directions on the same set of dimensions: career direction, core work and output, key differences, and which direction better fits each preference. Adjacent directions are described according to their own official occupational descriptions and do not mean job titles are interchangeable.

Evidence note: the career directions and core outputs are based on the official descriptions of O*NET 15-1299.07 and the related occupations list, under the U.S. definition; the education, qualification, and authorization requirements of adjacent occupations must be verified separately by their own jurisdictions, and this page does not write any direction as a shortcut for a career change.

The table below compares blockchain engineers with adjacent occupations and the pathways for moving in from adjacent positions; the basis for judgment is the main output, the object of responsibility, and the required training, not how similar the job titles are.
Information Security Analysts (15-1212.00)
Directed at organizational information system security protection, with outputs mainly being security policies, monitoring alerts, vulnerability handling, and compliance assessments.

Both focus on security, but information security analysts cover protection and compliance for the entire information system, while the default subject of blockchain engineers is the implementation and deployment security of distributed ledgers, cryptographic protocols, and smart contracts; protocol-level cryptographic design and testing are the more concentrated part of the latter.

If you want to cover broader security operations and compliance work, consider information security analysis first; if your interest is concentrated in ledger protocols, keys, and contract security, consider blockchain engineering first.
Computer Systems Analysts (15-1211.00)
Study an organization's existing systems and design improvements, with outputs mainly being requirements analysis, system design, and implementation recommendations.

Computer systems analysts center on business system analysis and improvement and usually do not go deep into cryptography and consensus implementation; blockchain engineers center on the technical implementation and deployment of protocols, nodes, and contracts and must handle distributed consistency and key management.

If you would rather do business process analysis and system planning, compare systems analysis first; if you would rather work on protocol and code implementation, consider blockchain engineering first.
Database Administrators (15-1242.00)
Design, organize, and protect data storage systems, with outputs mainly being data models, backup and recovery, and access control.

Both care about data integrity and access control, but database administrators work around centrally manageable storage systems, while blockchain engineers face distributed ledgers that are hard to modify after the fact and are maintained jointly by multiple parties; immutability and consensus mechanisms are constraints specific to the latter.

If you would rather work around data storage, queries, and backups, consider the database direction first; if you want to handle the constraints created by immutability and multi-party consensus, consider blockchain engineering first.
Computer Programmers (15-1251.00)
Write and test code to specification, with outputs mainly being runnable software modules and tests.

Computer programmers center on writing and testing code and usually are not responsible for system-level protocol design, key management, and distributed deployment; blockchain engineers must take on protocol and deployment security responsibility at the same time, and code is only one part of it.

If you would rather focus on coding and implementation, consider the programmer direction first; if you are willing to take on design, deployment, and security responsibility at the same time, consider blockchain engineering first.
Penetration Testers (15-1299.04)
Simulate attacks within an authorized scope, with outputs mainly being vulnerability discovery, exploitation validation, and remediation recommendations.

Penetration testing assesses systems from an attacker's perspective within authorized boundaries, while blockchain engineers design and deploy systems from a builder's perspective and do security and performance testing in a controlled environment; the directions of responsibility and the authorization boundaries differ.

If you enjoy the process of finding and exploiting vulnerabilities more, compare penetration testing first; if you would rather design and maintain systems that run over the long term, consider blockchain engineering first.
Moving in from software development or operations positions
You already have coding, deployment, or operations experience and want to move toward distributed ledgers and cryptographic protocols.

The gap is usually not programming ability but cryptographic protocols, consensus and distributed systems, key management, smart contract security, and change and rollback discipline; writing code that runs is not the same as being able to bear responsibility for production funds and data security.

If you are willing to build up the cryptography and distributed systems foundations and accept code review, you can consider moving in; if you only want to change the job title without building security and protocol training, the gap will be large.

Conclusion: the basis for choosing a direction is the main output, the object of responsibility, and the required technical training, not how similar the names are; once the direction is set, verify item by item the target direction's education requirements, the actual languages and toolchains used, access authorization for the production environment and keys, and the review mechanism for code and changes, and keep written confirmation.

paragraphs: Students or career changers preparing to enter this occupation

Editorial task suggestion: first complete, on a testnet or in a self-built environment, one closed loop from the requirements and threat list through design, implementation, testing, deployment, and rollback, and only then discuss tools and certificates; at the same time, verify whether the target position belongs to software and information technology services, financial technology, an internet platform, or blockchain information services, because the four differ in data permissions, release approval, and compliance requirements.
Working blockchain engineering personnel

Editorial task suggestion: use generative tools for rollback-capable steps such as code drafts and completion, first drafts of unit tests, log and document organization, and contract comments and examples; protocol and design pattern choices, the key and permission model, deployment and rollback plans, and security conclusions must remain with people.
Institutions and engineering teams

Editorial task suggestion: before introducing tools, clarify the usable steps, the knowledge scope and confidentiality requirements for code and contracts, access control for the production environment and keys, the review and source verification process for generated content, error escalation paths, and the responsible person for human review, so that any output returns to a version-controlled code repository.
Education and training

Editorial task suggestion: focus training on cryptographic protocols and consensus, distributed systems, keys and access control, code review and change discipline, and test design and fault injection, while also training vulnerability identification in generated code, dependency risk checking, and the ability to express uncertainty.

Editorial reasoning from the tasks: tools can assist code and test drafts and log and document organization; the materials read this round give no causal data on overall replacement, adoption, or time savings for this occupation, so perpetual non-replacement cannot be inferred. Global occupational task exposure to generative AI

The ILO 2025 methodology built an exposure gradient from a representative sample of 29,753 occupational tasks, a survey of 1,640 people, and 52,558 data points; the report notes that most occupations consist of tasks requiring human input, that the most likely impact is job transformation rather than wholesale replacement, and that the index does not provide job count predictions for a single occupation.

Editorial suggestion: trial AI-assisted search, code drafts, test samples, and log organization on fictional data, recording the time, errors, and manual changes, and only then judge whether time is saved; a speed-up must not be treated as already verified in advance. You need to build up network protocols, topology design, capacity planning, and failure recovery; ledger application experience is not the same as network architecture ability.

values: Fictional local ledger scenario

Simulated only on paper or in local memory, with no network, no funds, and no real keys; the initial state is ledger=[], writer_epoch=1, and the set of committed request_id values is empty. The writer role may only append, admin may only rotate, and reader may only read; the writer labels W1/W2 represent generations 1 and 2 respectively, and the admin label A is only a fictional input and does not provide real authentication security.

Event fields are (request_id,role,tag,action,payload). Input in order: E1=(r1,writer,W1,append,10); E2=(r1,writer,W1,append,10); E3=(r2,reader,R,append,20); E4=(r3,admin,A,rotate,2); E5=(r4,writer,W1,append,20); E6=(r5,writer,W2,append,20); E7=(r6,writer,W2,append,30, with an exception injected before commit). rotate may only change the epoch to the current epoch +1; append payloads may only be integers.

120 minutes in total: 40 minutes for the rules and threat list, 50 minutes for the simulated implementation, and 30 minutes for event-by-event testing and limitation statements. Any familiar language may be used for the implementation, and a complete paper trace is also acceptable; extra installations and cloud accounts are not necessary.
Rules and deliverables

First check whether the role is allowed to perform the action; if not, return DENIED and record one alert. After allowing append, check the writer tag against the current epoch; if invalid, return STALE and record an alert; then check the committed request_id and return DUPLICATE if it already exists; finally add the payload to a temporary copy and commit atomically, registering the request_id at the same time. On an exception, return FAILED, record an alert, and leave the ledger and the committed set unchanged. rotate is performed by admin A, adding 1 to the epoch and returning ROTATED without writing to the ledger; DENIED, STALE, DUPLICATE, and FAILED all do not write to the ledger.

Submit a seven-row results table (event, return code, ledger after handling, epoch, committed IDs, alerts), the permission matrix, runnable functions, and tests or a complete paper trace; explain why the idempotency check cannot bypass current permissions, and how to handle the case where the same r6 is retried after E7 with the injection canceled.
Reference answers and review

E1: APPENDED, [10], epoch1, {r1}; E2: DUPLICATE, [10], epoch1, {r1}; E3: DENIED, [10], epoch1, {r1}; E4: ROTATED, [10], epoch2, {r1}; E5: STALE, [10], epoch2, {r1}; E6: APPENDED, [10,20], epoch2, {r1,r5}; E7: FAILED, [10,20], epoch2, {r1,r5}. Alerts are one each for E3, E5, and E7, and the log records only the event ID, role, action, and result, not the tag; 3 alerts in total.

E7 did not register r6, so after canceling the injection a retry of the same event should be APPENDED with ledger=[10,20,30], epoch2, and committed set={r1,r5,r6}, with the alert count still 3. Minimum verification: all seven rows are consistent, failures leave no residual payload or ID, W1 becomes invalid after rotation, and duplicate requests are not written twice. This exercise is only a permission, idempotency, and atomicity model and does not implement cryptographic signatures, distributed consensus, or immutability guarantees.
Limitation and risk statements

Write at least three limitations: tag comparison is not security authentication, a single-process memory model has no multi-node consensus, and the data do not persist across process restarts. You may add unverified items such as network partitions, concurrent races, and cryptographic proofs; do not rewrite APPENDED or passing tests as production security conclusions, and do not connect to mainnet or real accounts.

List education, training, service applicability scope, and institutional permissions by target jurisdiction; attach a specific source, data period, and gaps to each item, plus the writer, admin, and reader permission matrix from this exercise.
Do not merge degrees, technical proficiency assessments, public information service filing, and institutional production permissions.

Submit the results table for E1 to E7 and for the E7 retry, compare it row by row with the reference answers, and keep the before-and-after differences of your corrections.

You may ask an experienced person to review; when no one is available, review against the answers yourself and note that no external review was obtained, since the seven-day experience does not depend on someone else being free.

Explain the requirements, the validation order, the E7 atomicity, the W1 invalidation, the duplicate r1, and the three limitations, with a decision to continue or pause.
Distinguish verified local behavior, model assumptions, and cryptographic authentication, consensus, and persistence that are not yet implemented, and do not claim production security.

paragraphs: Qualification boundary: education, proof of skills, institutional authorization, production and key permissions, and release responsibility are five different statuses, and none can be inferred automatically from another.

U.S. side: O*NET lists this occupation as Job Zone Four (SVP 7.0 to less than 8.0), and respondents consider a bachelor's degree necessary at 38%, some college education without a degree at 19%, and a master's degree at 13%; the O*NET education and training information is not a list of occupational licenses, and entry conditions must be verified separately by the target jurisdiction, service content, and employer requirements.

Item 86 of the 2026 public notice by the Fuzhou Human Resources and Social Security Bureau actually lists blockchain engineering technicians (2-02-38-08); when the Cyberspace Administration of China republished it in 2020 the code was 2-02-10-15, describing architecture, underlying technology, applications, testing, deployment, and operations. The original 2022 code entry returned no body text this round, and no claim is made that the full text was read. Classification is not the same as an individual license, and a same-named Chinese position does not prove one-to-one correspondence with U.S. 15-1299.07. Editorial suggestion: access production systems and keys within a written authorization scope and adopt least privilege; the Provisions on the Administration of Blockchain Information Services apply to entities, nodes, and related technical support organizations that provide blockchain information services to the public; filing is required within ten working days from the date the service is provided, security assessment must be reported to procedure when developing and launching new products, applications, or functions, and real-name authentication, content management, and log backups of no less than six months must be implemented. Filing is not an individual occupational license, and not all internal ledger development should be treated as a public information service.

Before applying and starting, verify item by item education recognition, course and training content, production and key permissions, and review and release rules, and keep written confirmation. The related training directory has 3,657 items, based on the IPEDS2025—26 institution directory, 2024—25 degrees awarded, and CIP mapping, and covers computing and related programs; these are not 3,657 blockchain-specific courses or real-time enrollment, and specific eligibility, program length, costs, and open apprenticeships were not verified. The O*NET related directory lists 1 item, EC-Council Certified Blockchain Professional (CBP), which requires an examination, and the directory Q and A states recertification through CEUs every 3 years; it is not an entry license for all engineers. The vendor's current page presents CBP together with BDC, BFC, and BBLC, and BDC recommends object-oriented, asynchronous JavaScript, and front-end and back-end development foundations; this cannot be used to determine the CBP examination branch. CBP's specific eligibility, examination fee, total training cost, recertification hours and fees, and current registration availability remain insufficient evidence, and other certificates with the same abbreviation are not conflated.

Insufficient evidence: the bounded search this round did not obtain a specific blockchain engineering job posting that allows simultaneous verification of posting date, duties, education, and pay; the O*NET group profile and the editorially drafted position table are not packaged as real recruitment samples.
